issues.legal_issue: An application to reject a plaint for failure to disclose a cause of action must be decided from the plaint’s averments, without relying on the defendant’s defence.
material_facts: The owner applied under Order VII Rule 11 on the ground that the plaint disclosed no cause of action against it.
The plaintiff relied on material outside the plaint in support of its claim, and the applications concerning rejection, amendment and interim relief were considered together.
issues.conclusion: The application had to be decided on the plaint averments alone; the defendant’s written statement and other material outside the plaint were irrelevant to that inquiry. The power may be exercised at any stage before the conclusion of the trial.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(a) and (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court examines the plaint and not the defence when deciding whether it discloses a cause of action or appears barred by law. The power may be exercised at any stage before trial concludes: Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra; Raptakos Brett & Co. Ltd. v. Ganesh Property; Mayar (H.K.) Ltd. v. Owners & Parties, Vessel M.V. Fortune Express. A meaningful, rather than merely formal, reading is required, and a meritless plaint that creates only an illusion of a cause of action should be rejected: T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal.

predicates.application_to_reject_plaint: A defendant asks the court to reject a plaint in a civil suit.
predicates.cause_of_action_ground: The application asserts that the plaint does not disclose a cause of action.
predicates.apparent_legal_bar: The application asserts that the plaint itself shows that the suit is barred by law.

issues.definition: When a defendant seeks rejection of a plaint for lack of a cause of action or an apparent legal bar, the court decides that application using the plaint’s averments alone.

issues.legal_issue: A specific-performance plaint does not disclose a cause of action against a property owner when it relies on an intermediary’s authority to contract for the owner but omits the material authority and agreement particulars needed to establish that authority.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought specific performance of an agreement made with an intermediary, alleging that the intermediary was the owner’s agreement-holder and registered power-of-attorney holder.
The plaint did not set out the terms or date of the alleged agreement between the owner and the intermediary, and that agreement was not produced.
The plaintiff did not produce the power of attorney or explain whose custody it was in, and did not provide a registration copy.

The power of attorney produced for consideration authorized specified acts of representation before statutory authorities, but did not authorize an agreement of sale, execution of a sale deed, or admission of execution before the Registrar.
issues.conclusion: The plaint did not disclose a complete cause of action against the owner, and its rejection against the owner was correctly ordered.
issues.legal_principle: Order VII Rule 11(a) requires rejection where the plaint does not disclose a cause of action. A cause of action is the bundle of material facts which, with the applicable law, gives a right to relief and must include an act of the defendant: A.B.C. Laminart Pvt. Ltd. v. A.P. Agencies and Bloom Dekor Ltd. v. Subhash Himatlal Desai. Under Order VII Rule 14(1) and (2), the plaintiff must produce documents on which the claim is based or state whose custody they are in; Forms 47 and 48 in Appendix A require material particulars for a specific-performance claim, including the agreement date. Where limitation is in issue, Order VII Rule 6 requires the basis for exemption to be pleaded. A power of attorney is strictly construed and authorizes only the acts granted; authority to agree to sell or effect a sale must be expressly given. This is consistent with Sections 1-A and 2 of the Powers of Attorney Act, 1882, Chapter X of the Contract Act, 1872, and Suraj Lamp and Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Haryana, which discusses State of Rajasthan v. Basant Nahata. The court also referred to U.S. Sasidharan v. K. Karunakaran and Manohar Joshi v. Nitin Bhaurao Patil on incorporation by reference of documents whose terms are referred to in a plaint, and to Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, on the discretionary nature of specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and agreement_with_intermediary_claimed_to_bind_owner and authority_terms_not_pleaded_or_produced and power_of_attorney_not_produced_or_explained and authority_limited_to_non_sale_acts and agreement_date_omitted

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.agreement_with_intermediary_claimed_to_b: The plaintiff relies on an agreement with an intermediary and alleges that the intermediary could bind the property owner.
predicates.authority_terms_not_pleaded_or_produced: The plaintiff neither pleads the material terms of the intermediary’s authority from the owner nor produces the document establishing that authority.
predicates.power_of_attorney_not_produced_or_explai: The plaintiff does not produce the alleged power of attorney or explain whose custody it is in.
predicates.authority_limited_to_non_sale_acts: The authority document relied on permits specified acts other than agreeing to sell or completing a sale of the property.
predicates.agreement_date_omitted: The plaint omits the date of the agreement on which the specific-performance claim is based.

issues.definition: If a specific-performance claim against an owner depends on an intermediary’s authority, but the authority and agreement particulars are missing and the instrument relied on does not authorize a sale, the plaint is rejected against the owner for failure to disclose a cause of action.

issues.legal_issue: A co-defendant against whom no relief is sought need not be joined to an application by another defendant for rejection of the plaint.
material_facts: The owner applied to reject the plaint and sought no relief against the intermediary who was the second defendant in the suit.
The objection that the intermediary had not been joined in the rejection application was raised, but the intermediary’s rights were not affected by deciding that application.
The rejection application could be decided before summons was issued.
issues.conclusion: The intermediary was not a necessary party to the application for rejection of the plaint, and the non-joinder objection was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: An application under Order VII Rule 11 may be decided before registration of the plaint or issuance of summons, and other defendants need not necessarily be heard where their rights are unaffected: Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra. A party against whom no relief is sought in the application is not a necessary party. An objection to non-joinder should be raised in the trial court so that the defect can be addressed; it cannot ordinarily be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court where it was not raised below and has not caused a failure of justice: State of U.P. v. Ram Swarup Saroj.

rule.if: application_to_reject_plaint and co_defendant_not_joined and no_relief_sought_against_co_defendant and decision_does_not_affect_co_defendant_rights

predicates.application_to_reject_plaint: A defendant applies for rejection of a plaint in a civil suit.
predicates.co_defendant_not_joined: Another defendant in the suit is not joined to that application.
predicates.no_relief_sought_against_co_defendant: The application seeks no relief against the defendant who was not joined.
predicates.decision_does_not_affect_co_defendant_ri: Deciding the rejection application does not affect the rights of the defendant who was not joined.

issues.definition: A co-defendant need not be joined to an application to reject a plaint when the application seeks no relief against that co-defendant and its decision does not affect that defendant’s rights.
